# Hyperkalemia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Fluids, electrolytes, and acid-base disorders > Hyperkalemia*

[Original Article Link](/library/7g0492)

---

## Summary

Hyperkalemia (high serum <u>potassium</u>) is a common and potentially life-threatening disorder of <u>potassium</u> balance. The most common cause is decreased <u>kidney function</u>. It can also be caused by <u>acidosis</u>, cell breakdown, endocrinological disturbances (e.g., <u>hypoaldosteronism</u>, <u>hypocortisolism</u>), and drugs such as <u>potassium-sparing diuretics</u>, <u>angiotensin-converting enzyme</u> (<u>ACE</u>) inhibitors, <u>nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs</u> (<u>NSAIDs</u>), and <u>digoxin</u>. Serum <u>potassium</u> (<u>K<sup>+</sup></u>) is often falsely elevated due to the method of sampling and levels should be confirmed with repeat testing. To determine the underlying cause of hyperkalemia, it is essential to review the patient's medications, check <u>kidney</u> and endocrine function, and screen for cell lysis (e.g., <u>hemolysis</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>) and <u>acid-base disorders</u>. Acute increases in serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> are very dangerous, as they influence the <u>resting membrane potential</u> and thus the electrical excitability of cells. These changes can lead to life-threatening <u>cardiac arrhythmias</u>. It is, therefore, essential to obtain an <u>ECG</u> to determine the level of cardiotoxicity. Management depends on the severity of the hyperkalemia and includes restriction of dietary <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, as well as medications to bind, shift, or eliminate <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, or to stabilize the cardiac membrane (e.g., <u>calcium gluconate</u>) if necessary. In refractory cases, dialysis may be required. Serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> should be monitored closely until it is corrected.




See also “<u>Hypokalemia</u>.”




![Hyperkalemia fact sheet](media/acmoocv6n4aay401umfnrbsg.jpg)

Hyperkalemia fact sheet

---

## Definitions

* Hyperkalemia: Serum <u>potassium</u> level > 5 mEq/L

* Acute hyperkalemia: Abnormal ↑ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> not known to be chronic

* Chronic hyperkalemia: Recurrent episodic ↑ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> that require ongoing treatment





References: [[1]](/library/-o0DeS)[[2]](/library/bkXHmy)

---

## Etiology

* <u>Potassium</u> excess: due to altered <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> metabolism or intake

* Reduced excretion: acute and <u>chronic kidney disease</u> [[3]](/library/XK09US)

* Endocrine causes: <u>hypocortisolism</u>, <u>hypoaldosteronism</u>

* Drugs: <u>potassium-sparing diuretics</u>, <u>ACE inhibitors</u>, <u>angiotensin receptor blockers</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, and <u>trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole</u>  [[4]](/library/bK0HUS)

* <u>Type IV renal tubular acidosis</u>

* Increased intake

* High <u>potassium</u> diet, e.g., fresh fruits, dried fruits and legumes, vegetables, nuts, seeds, bran products, milk, and dairy products

* <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> containing <u>IV fluids</u>

* Extracellular shift

* <u>Acidosis</u> → ↑ extracellular H<sup>+</sup> → inhibition of the <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> antiporter</u> → ↓ intracellular Na<sup>+</sup> → ↓ <u>sodium</u> gradient inhibits the <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase</u> → ↑ extracellular <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> concentration ;  [[5]](/library/bwcHhe0)

* Hyperkalemia → ↑ extracellular <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> concentration → ↑ <u>potassium</u> gradient stimulates the <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase</u> → ↑ extracellular Na<sup>+</sup> → ↑ <u>sodium</u> gradient stimulates the <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> antiporter</u> → ↑ extracellular H<sup>+</sup> → <u>acidosis</u>

* Exceptions: In <u>renal tubular acidosis</u> and <u>acetazolamide</u> toxicity, findings include <u>hypokalemia</u> and <u>metabolic acidosis</u>.

* <u>Hyperosmolality</u>

* <u>Insulin</u> deficiency (manifests with <u>hyperglycemia</u>)

* Drugs

* <u>Beta blockers</u>

* <u>Succinylcholine</u>: (esp. when given with preexisting <u>burns</u> and/or muscle trauma) ,

* <u>Digoxin</u>: inhibits the <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase</u> → ↑ extracellular <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> concentration

* Extracellular release

* Pathological cell lysis

* <u>Rhabdomyolysis</u>

* <u>Tumor lysis syndrome</u>

* <u>Hemolysis</u>

* High blood cell turnover: e.g., <u>thrombocytosis</u>, <u>erythrocytosis</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>

* Pseudohyperkalemia: resulting from <u>iatrogenic</u> <u>red blood cell</u> lysis

* Blood drawn from the side of IV infusion or a <u>central line</u> without previous flushing

* Prolonged use of a <u>tourniquet</u>

* Fist clenching during blood withdrawal

* Delayed sample analysis





> [!WARNING]
> Errors in blood-drawing technique may lead to <u>red blood cell</u> lysis and a falsely elevated serum <u>potassium</u> concentration (<u>pseudohyperkalemia</u>)!




> [!NOTE]
> When K<sup>+</sup> shifts out of <u>the cell</u>, it's a BAD LOSS! – Beta blockers, Acidosis, Digoxin, Lysis, hyperOsmolality, high Sugar, Succinylcholine




References:[[4]](/library/bK0HUS)[[6]](/library/cK0a2S)

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Potassium</u> is an important factor in maintaining the <u>resting membrane potential</u>

* ↑ Extracellular <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>concentration → resting membrane potential becomes less negative than -90 mV → ↑ excitability





> [!NOTE]
> Particularly acute extracellular changes in concentration influence excitability! Chronic changes lead to intracellular compensation!

---

## Clinical features

Symptoms usually occur if serum <u>potassium</u> levels are > 7.0 mEq/L or they change rapidly.




* <u>Cardiac arrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>atrioventricular block</u>, <u>ventricular fibrillation</u>)

* <u>Muscle weakness</u>, <u>paralysis</u>, <u>paresthesia</u>

* ↓ Deep <u>tendon reflexes</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Hyperkalemia (and <u>hypokalemia</u>) can cause <u>cardiac arrhythmia</u> and lead to <u>ventricular fibrillation</u>!References:[[1]](/library/-o0DeS)[[7]](/library/ph0LUf)[[8]](/library/WK0P2S)[[9]](/library/dK0o2S)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[10]](/library/WucPJV0)




* Obtain routine <u>laboratory studies</u> to:

* Confirm hyperkalemia and severity.

* Assess renal function.

* Evaluate <u>etiology of hyperkalemia</u>.

* Check <u>ECG</u>: Urgent treatment is required for <u>ECG changes in hyperkalemia</u>.

* Inquire about last <u>renal replacement therapy</u> for patients with <u>ESRD</u> (e.g., screen for missed <u>hemodialysis</u> appointments, adherence to <u>peritoneal dialysis</u>).

* Send further diagnostic laboratory testing depending on the suspected underlying etiology.





![Management of hyperkalemia](media/witqy1c3ld9gdjsc6epyn2kk.jpg)

Management of hyperkalemia




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[11]](/library/wcXheC)[[12]](/library/HdXKrC)




* <u>BMP</u>

* <u>Glucose</u>: If very high, consider spurious hyperkalemia secondary to <u>hyperglycemic crisis</u>.

* Serum <u>electrolytes</u> 

* Na<sup>+</sup>: normal or can be ↓ in <u>adrenal insufficiency</u> (see “Diagnostics” in “<u>Adrenal insufficiency</u>”)

* <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>: Repeat to confirm the diagnosis and rule out <u>pseudohyperkalemia</u> (see “Etiology”).

* <u>Renal function tests</u>: often show renal impairment  [[13]](/library/GcXBdC)

* <u>CBC</u>: can show <u>hemolytic anemia</u> or <u>thrombocytosis</u>  [[14]](/library/1QX2EB)

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>: may be abnormal in <u>hemolysis</u> or <u>tumor lysis syndrome</u>

* Blood gases:  (venous or arterial): often show <u>metabolic acidosis</u>  [[15]](/library/yUXdfx)





> [!NOTE]
> An inverse relationship between serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> and <u>pH</u> (e.g., ↓ <u>pH</u> → ↑ <u>K+</u>) has previously been observed in specific types of <u>metabolic acidosis</u>. However, the underlying mechanisms are complex and this association is inconsistent in clinical practice. [[11]](/library/wcXheC)[[15]](/library/yUXdfx)




### ECG findings in hyperkalemia [[16]](/library/11X2fC)[[17]](/library/1dX2KC)[[18]](/library/SdXy6C)




There is a weak <u>correlation</u> between serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> levels and the severity of <u>ECG</u> changes. Findings are more likely to occur with rapid-onset hyperkalemia.




* Mild hyperkalemia: 5.5–6.4 mEq/L 
* Tall, peaked <u>T waves</u>

* Moderate hyperkalemia: 6.5–8.0 mEq/L  

* Lengthening of QRS interval (<u>QRS complex</u> widening)

* Widening and flattening of <u>P wave</u>, which eventually disappears

* Severe hyperkalemia: > 8.0 mEq/L  

* Absent <u>P wave</u>

* Intraventricular conduction block

* Unusual QRS morphology

* Sine wave pattern: a sinusoidal pattern with absent <u>P waves</u> and a wide <u>QRS complex</u> that merges with the <u>T wave</u>; a marker of impending V-Fib and <u>asystole</u>

* <u>Cardiac arrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>V-tach</u>, <u>V-fib</u>), <u>asystole</u>

### Investigation of underlying causes [[19]](/library/5zaitM)[[20]](/library/TSX6_x)[[21]](/library/gSXF_x)




Depending on symptoms and <u>risk factors</u>, further testing may be appropriate, particularly if renal function is normal.




* <u>Creatine kinase</u>: ↑ in <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>

* <u>LDH</u>: ↑ in <u>tumor lysis syndrome</u> or <u>hemolysis</u>

* <u>Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system</u>

* ↑ <u>Aldosterone</u>: suggestive of, e.g., <u>pseudohypoaldosteronism</u> or nephropathy due to <u>sickle cell disease</u>

* ↓ <u>Aldosterone</u>: Assess <u>plasma renin activity</u> or plasma <u>renin</u> concentration (see also “<u>Hypoaldosteronism</u>”).

* Normal or ↑ <u>renin</u>; : suggests, e.g., <u>hypoaldosteronism</u> (e.g., due to <u>Addison disease</u>) or <u>congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>

* ↓ <u>Renin</u>: suggests, e.g., <u>AIN</u>, <u>diabetic nephropathy</u>

* <u>Cortisol</u>: can be ↓ in <u>primary adrenal insufficiency</u> (see “<u>Endocrine testing for adrenal insufficiency</u>”)

* Urine <u>electrolytes</u>: rarely indicated  [[22]](/library/aQXQuB)





> [!TIP]
> Review the patient's <u>medical history</u> and medication list to help identify potential <u>causes of hyperkalemia</u>. [[19]](/library/5zaitM)

---

## Treatment

![Management of hyperkalemia](media/witqy1c3ld9gdjsc6epyn2kk.jpg)

Management of hyperkalemia




### Therapeutic approach to hyperkalemia [[2]](/library/bkXHmy)[[11]](/library/wcXheC)[[19]](/library/5zaitM)[[23]](/library/ekbx5F)




* Determine severity: See “Risk <u>stratification</u>.”

* <u>Hyperkalemic emergency</u>: Patients require immediate management.

* Start <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>.

* If there are <u>ECG</u> changes: Stabilize the cardiac membrane first, e.g., with IV <u>calcium gluconate</u>.

* Initiate treatment to shift <u>potassium</u> intracellularly, e.g.:

* <u>Short-acting insulin</u> with <u>glucose</u>

* Consider the addition of inhaled <u>SABAs</u>.

* Consider nephrology and critical care consults.

* Admit to hospital for ongoing monitoring and treatment.

* Repeat serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> at minimum 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 hours after treatment.

* All patients

* Identify and treat underlying causes.

* <u>Review medications</u> and discontinue or modify dosing of medications that may be contributing to hyperkalemia.

* Decrease dose (or consider discontinuation) of drugs required to treat underlying conditions, e.g., <u>RAAS inhibitors</u>.

* Avoid nonessential drugs associated with hyperkalemia (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>, over-the-counter supplements such as milkweed).

* Start a low <u>potassium</u> diet and avoid salt substitutes (consider nutrition consult).  [[12]](/library/HdXKrC)[[24]](/library/QPXuey)

* Consider treatment to remove <u>potassium</u> from the body, e.g., <u>cation-exchange resins</u>, <u>diuretics</u>, <u>hemodialysis</u>.

* Repeat <u>potassium</u> regularly until it is within normal range, e.g., within 1–3 days.   [[25]](/library/KEcU9V0)





> [!WARNING]
> Urgent <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>-lowering treatment may be necessary even in the absence of <u>ECG</u> changes.




> [!NOTE]
> To remember <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>-lowering treatments, think C BIG K Die (if you see a big serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, your patient may die!): Calcium salts, Beta-<u>agonists</u>/Bicarbonate, Insulin + Glucose, Kation exchange medication, Dialysis/Diuretics.




> [!TIP]
> The effects of <u>calcium</u> salts, <u>insulin</u>/<u>glucose</u>, and inhaled <u>SABAs</u> on serum <u>K+</u> are temporary. Repeat doses may be required while waiting for interventions to remove <u>K+</u> from the body to take effect.




### Risk <u>stratification</u> [[26]](/library/SVXyFC)




* Hyperkalemic emergency is an acute severe elevation that requires urgent lowering and occurs if any of the following are present:

* Clinical manifestations: e.g., <u>ECG changes in hyperkalemia</u>, <u>muscle weakness</u>, <u>paralysis</u>

* Serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> 6.0–6.5 mEq/L  [[27]](/library/OVXIuC)

* Comorbidities that affect ongoing <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> influx and elimination: e.g., <u>AKI</u>, <u>ESRD</u>, <u>GI bleeding</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>, <u>TLS</u>

* <u>Less urgent hyperkalemia</u> (typically chronic elevations that can be lowered more slowly)

* Patient is asymptomatic

* Serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> is 5.5–6.0 mEq/L

* Patient has no high-risk comorbidities





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Cardiac arrhythmias</u> due to hyperkalemia can cause sudden <u>death</u>.




### Cardiac membrane stabilization [[23]](/library/ekbx5F)




<u>Calcium</u> salts reduce cardiac irritability.




* Indication: <u>ECG changes in hyperkalemia</u>

* Options

* 10% <u>calcium gluconate</u> DOSAGE  [[26]](/library/SVXyFC)

* 10% <u>calcium</u> <u>chloride</u> (preferably given in a central or <u>deep vein</u>) DOSAGE  [[19]](/library/5zaitM)

* Considerations [[11]](/library/wcXheC)

* Ensure <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u> throughout to detect potential <u>arrhythmias</u>.

* Effects last only 30–60 minutes; additional dosing may be required.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Calcium</u> salts should result in normalization of the <u>ECG</u> appearance within 5 minutes; observe the <u>cardiac monitor</u> following initial treatment and repeat the dose if the <u>ECG</u> tracing still appears abnormal.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Calcium</u> salts have no influence on serum <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> levels and therefore should be paired with a <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>-lowering agent.




### Intracellular <u>potassium</u> shifting [[11]](/library/wcXheC)[[26]](/library/SVXyFC)[[28]](/library/ZeXZxC)




These drugs should be given in tandem with <u>calcium</u> salts (if <u>calcium</u> is indicated).




* <u>Insulin</u> and <u>glucose</u>

* Preferred acute noninvasive <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>-lowering treatment

* Sample agent: short-acting <u>insulin</u> combined with <u>50% dextrose</u> DOSAGE

* Patients with <u>glucose</u> levels > 250 mg/dL should not receive <u>D50W</u>.

* Monitor all patients for <u>hypoglycemia</u> hourly for at least 2 hours after administration.

* Inhaled <u>SABAs</u>

* Consider as an adjunct to <u>insulin</u> (not effective as a monotherapy).  [[23]](/library/ekbx5F)[[29]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Sample agent: <u>nebulized</u> <u>albuterol</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE

* <u>Sodium bicarbonate</u>

* Consider as an adjunct treatment only in patients with severe <u>metabolic acidosis</u>;  (i.e., <u>pH</u> < 7.2).

* There is no evidence to support using <u>bicarbonate</u> in the <u>management of hyperkalemia</u> in nonacidotic patients.

* Recommended concentration is IV 8.4% <u>sodium bicarbonate</u> DOSAGE [[28]](/library/ZeXZxC)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid administering <u>calcium carbonate</u> and <u>sodium</u> <u>chloride</u> through the same IV line without extensive flushing in between because of the risk of <u>calcium</u> precipitation. [[30]](/library/Tvc6zV0)




### Enhanced <u>potassium</u> elimination [[2]](/library/bkXHmy)[[23]](/library/ekbx5F)[[28]](/library/ZeXZxC)




* Not required for all patients; treatment of the underlying cause may be sufficient.

* The choice of treatment depends on underlying medical conditions and <u>volume status</u>.





#### Cation-exchange medications [[26]](/library/SVXyFC)[[31]](/library/HfXKnx)




* Mechanism of action: These drugs release Na<sup>+</sup> or <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> ions in the gut, which are exchanged for <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, thereby enhancing enteral <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> elimination.

* Clinical applications: nonurgent lowering of <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>  [[11]](/library/wcXheC)

* Options

* <u>Cation-exchange resins</u> 

* Sodium polystyrene sulfonate DOSAGE: falling out of favor due to adverse effects

* <u>Sodium</u> zirconium cyclosilicate DOSAGE

* <u>Cation-exchange polymers</u>, e.g., patiromer DOSAGE  [[32]](/library/EfX8Lx)

* Adverse effects

* Gastrointestinal upset

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* Considerations

* Avoid simultaneous administration with other oral medications, as resins may bind them, reducing absorption.

* Give with a <u>laxative</u> (avoid <u>sorbitol</u>).  [[33]](/library/YQXnuB)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Sodium polystyrene sulfonate</u> carries a risk of intestinal <u>necrosis</u> (especially if combined with the <u>laxative</u> <u>sorbitol</u>) and should be avoided in patients with abnormal bowel function. [[33]](/library/YQXnuB)




#### <u>Hemodialysis</u>




* Most effective definitive therapy for refractory hyperkalemia

* Preferred option in patients with <u>end-stage renal failure</u> ; (particularly if already receiving <u>renal replacement therapy</u>), or <u>oliguria</u>.

* For all other patients, avoided as a first-line option because of its invasive nature and adverse effects





#### <u>Loop diuretics</u> [[28]](/library/ZeXZxC)




* Consider <u>loop diuretics</u>, e.g., <u>furosemide</u> DOSAGE for patients with <u>volume overload</u>

* Closely <u>monitor fluid balance</u> and <u>electrolytes</u> due to unpredictable effects and risk of <u>adverse events</u>.
